answer.exemplar: The index version can read any position, so a rule that compares neighbours is a two-line change: read position i - 1 beside position i, with the boundary at i = 0 handled by an IF. FOR EACH hands over only the current character, so the neighbour check has to be rebuilt by hand as a manual index, and that hand-rolled version is where off-by-one errors and an unguarded i - 1 at the start come from.

questions.explanation: A complete answer names what the index version can reach that the FOR EACH version cannot, and points at the specific hazards the manual workaround introduces: reading position minus 1 at the start and drifting out of step with the loop.
questions.hint: Ask which version can look at a position other than the current one.

Reading the positions in ascending order describes a loop reading word[i] rather than word[2 minus i], and stopping after one pass mistakes a three-pass loop for a single one.

questions.explanation: Building a copy leaves the stored value as it was, so the routine can compare the two, undo the change, or reuse the original in a later step. Assuming every change is equally cheap forgets that copying a long value copies every character, and assuming the copy is smaller has no basis, since the routine writes one character per pass.
questions.hint: Ask what the program can still do with the value it did not change.
